\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

All tables and figures in this section report values computed from the experimental runs.

\subsection{RQ1: Reasoning}
\label{sec:rq1}

Reasoning is evaluated on the paired sampled items, restricted to the \emph{tractable} items: those
whose reasoning runs never overflowed the 32\,768-token output ceiling, so a clean on-score exists.
The overflow exclusion removes 293 run rows (186 distinct items: 91 SemEval, 65 Mohler, 17 RIAYN, 13
PT-CS), all from Qwen with reasoning on. The
extractable rate $\pi$ is 1.0 everywhere else. Because
the overflowing items are the ones provoking the longest reasoning, the excluded items are not
random, and every claim in this subsection holds for the tractable items only.

\input{tables/tab_rq1_values}

Agreement gains are specific to the model and the dataset, never uniform: on the trade-off plane of
Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1trade} the points spread widely along the horizontal agreement axis ($\Delta$QWK is the
change in QWK from reasoning off to on). Table~\ref{tab:rq1values} gives every value. Reasoning
helped Qwen3.5 significantly on four of its five datasets (each percentage is the gain relative to
the reasoning-off QWK): Mohler ($\Delta$QWK $+0.071$, $+11$\%), SemEval ($+0.098$, $+18$\%), RIAYN
($+0.250$, $+45$\%), and PT-CS code ($+0.113$, $+23$\%). Its PT-CS short-answer gain ($+0.092$,
$+12$\%) is not significant. The only other significant gain is GPT-5.1 on RIAYN ($+0.228$, $+41$\%).
These five gains are judged one comparison at a time. Across all twenty model-dataset comparisons, some
would clear that bar by chance, so we also apply Holm's correction, which raises the bar for each
comparison in turn to keep the chance of any false positive at 5\%; after it, only the two RIAYN gains,
for Qwen3.5 and GPT-5.1, remain significant. Everywhere else no gain was detected. For two of those
cases the data go further: on Mohler, the gain for GLM-5.1 ($+0.005$) and GPT-5.1 ($+0.006$) is
equivalent to zero, meaning its 90\% interval lies inside the margin of $\pm0.05$ QWK that we fixed in
advance as too small to change any recommendation. The other intervals are too wide to call the two
settings equivalent, especially on PT-CS, where the comparisons rest on 25 to 67 items.

Reasoning's gains come at a price, and Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1trade} already shows the dominant pattern:
most points sit below the horizontal axis, so consistency falls even where agreement rises.
Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1} shows the same comparison as bars, one per model and dataset, and adds the token
cost, which Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1trade} does not show: panel~(a) gives the agreement change, panel~(b) the
consistency change, and panel~(c) the token cost. Reading one model on one dataset across the three
panels shows what reasoning bought and what it cost. The price has two parts.
First, tokens: reasoning multiplied completion tokens by 9 to 925 times, and the premium is
domain-conditional even within one model. GPT-5.1 costs 9 to 31 times as much on short answers but
146 to 211 times on code; Qwen3.5, whose traces are the longest, costs 666 to 925 times as much
(Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}c). A single overall span hides exactly the conditionality this study is about, so
the guide quotes the premium per domain. Second, consistency: the within-item SD across repetitions
rises from off to on in 17 of the 20 model-dataset combinations (it falls in three: GLM-5.1 on PT-CS
code, and GPT-5.1 on PT-CS short answers and on RIAYN), all at temperature 0 (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}b).
Reasoning therefore trades reproducibility for agreement even when the agreement gain itself is not
significant; Section~\ref{sec:discussion} unpacks how much of that loss is mechanical.

One code-specific failure shapes how the code results must be read. On PT-CS code, Qwen3.5
with reasoning off gives a score of exactly zero to 47\% of the answers, although the teachers gave
none of the same answers a zero. We call this behaviour the \emph{zero-collapse}: answers that
deserve partial credit receive the same score as an empty answer, so the grader can no longer tell
weak answers apart. A grader that instead spreads its scores across the scale, as the teachers do, we
call a \emph{discriminating} grader. The zeros are genuine, parseable scores that recur regardless of
scope.
Reasoning repairs the collapse for Qwen (the zero fraction falls to 24\%, and the $+0.113$ gain above
follows), so that gain is best read as repairing a broken baseline, not as evidence that reasoning helps
code grading in general. GPT-5.1 shows a milder form of the same behaviour: with reasoning off it gives a
zero to 32\% of the PT-CS code answers and 17\% of RIAYN's, against 2\% and 5\% for the teachers, and
its significant RIAYN gain fits that pattern. GLM-5.1 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, which give zero to 9 to
13\% of the answers, gained little from reasoning on either code dataset. The configuration guide (Section~\ref{sec:framework}) therefore
keys its code guidance on baseline behaviour rather than model identity.

Overall, reasoning emerges from RQ1 as a conditional trade rather than a default upgrade. It improved
agreement with teacher grades in only some model-dataset combinations, always at a large and domain-dependent
token cost, and usually at some loss of run-to-run consistency. Its one dependable use was repairing a
model that had collapsed to zero on code; absent that, the gains were small or uncertain enough that
turning reasoning on rarely pays for itself.

\subsection{RQ2: Evaluation Guidance}
\label{sec:rq2}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq2_guidance.pgf}
\caption{Evaluation-guidance benefit per dataset and model: the change in agreement ($\Delta$QWK, K=5,
with 95\% confidence intervals) when the reference answer or rubric is added on top of the question and
student answer. Reasoning off.}
\label{fig:rq2}
\end{figure}

Evaluation guidance adds the reference answer or rubric on top of the question and student answer. We
measured it on three model families, Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5.1, each with reasoning off,
on all four datasets (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq2}). The reference answer is the guidance for the short-answer
datasets (Mohler, SemEval) and the rubric for the code datasets (RIAYN, PT-CS code).

Guidance raised agreement in 11 of the 12 model-dataset combinations, and all eleven gains remain
significant after Holm's correction. The gains run from $+0.095$ QWK (DeepSeek-V4-Flash on Mohler) to
$+0.256$ (DeepSeek-V4-Flash on SemEval), that is, from about a sixth to three quarters above the
no-guidance level. They are similar on the deployment data: on the 295 PT-CS code answers the rubric
adds $+0.146$ for Qwen3.5, $+0.148$ for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and $+0.190$ for GPT-5.1. The one exception
is GPT-5.1 on RIAYN, where the rubric left agreement unchanged ($-0.005$, CI $[-0.13,+0.12]$).

Overall, evaluation guidance is the most consistent gain in the study: it held across three model
families and both domains, at the cost of only the extra prompt tokens. The practical reading is
simple: add a trustworthy rubric or reference answer whenever one exists.

\subsection{RQ3: Scope and Decomposition}
\label{sec:rq3}

A grade can be requested in more than one shape. Scope is whether the whole exam is graded in one
call or one question at a time; decomposition is whether each answer gets a single holistic score or
is scored criterion by criterion. In both, the model is shown the same criteria; criterion-by-criterion
scoring simply asks it to score each criterion separately and sum them, instead of giving one holistic
score. We compare each shape against the baseline, one question per call with a single holistic score,
on two model families, Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, with reasoning off (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq3}). Scope
needs complete exams, so it is measured on PT-CS code; decomposition is measured on PT-CS code and on
RIAYN, whose rubrics mark each step of one or more accepted solution paths.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq3_scope_decomp.pgf}
\caption{Scope and decomposition contrasts ($\Delta$QWK, K=5, with 95\% confidence intervals), per model:
grading the whole exam in one call instead of question by question (PT-CS code), and scoring criterion
by criterion instead of holistically (RIAYN and PT-CS code). Below zero means the alternative scored worse
than the baseline. Dashed lines mark the $\pm0.05$ equivalence margin. Reasoning off.}
\label{fig:rq3}
\end{figure}

PT-CS exams are short, about four questions each (median four, range one to six), so the whole-exam
call grades roughly four answers in one pass. Across the 295 PT-CS code questions, grading the whole
exam in one call lowered agreement for Qwen3.5 by $0.091$ QWK (CI $[-0.13,-0.05]$), about a fifth of
its question-by-question level of 0.468, and the loss remains significant after Holm's correction. For
DeepSeek-V4-Flash the change was $-0.024$ (CI $[-0.08,+0.03]$), not significant. Scoring criterion by
criterion never improved agreement either: the four changes run from $-0.072$ (DeepSeek-V4-Flash on PT-CS
code, significant after correction) to $+0.029$ (Qwen3.5 on RIAYN, not significant). Both contrasts are
scored against the final grade, per the design decision not to trust per-criterion human scores as
ground truth. None of the six intervals fits inside the $\pm0.05$ margin, so the data do not show the
shapes to be equivalent; they show that the alternatives never did better.

Cost does not favour the alternatives either. Per question, grading the whole exam in one call cost
Qwen3.5 7\% more than one call per question, because the joint answer carries more output tokens, and
scoring criterion by criterion cost about twice as much per answer as a single holistic score.

Overall, the baseline shape held its ground: grading one question per call with a single holistic
score was never beaten on agreement, and it was also the cheaper shape. Question-by-question, holistic
grading is therefore the default.

\subsection{RQ4: Models and Cost}
\label{sec:cost}

The four model families differ both in how well they grade and in what they cost. We read agreement per
dataset (Fig.~\ref{fig:perdataset}), then weigh it against cost task by task
(Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality}). The public datasets fall into two task types, short answer (Mohler and
SemEval) and code (RIAYN), so the two figures show the same evidence at two grains. On the public
datasets the eight configurations sit close together (mean QWK 0.590 to 0.667 across the three public
datasets), and the per-dataset winner changes (Fig.~\ref{fig:perdataset}): on Mohler it is Qwen3.5 with
reasoning on (0.659), on SemEval GLM-5.1 with reasoning off (0.621), and on RIAYN GLM-5.1 with reasoning
on (0.803).

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\input{figures/fig3_per_dataset_config.pgf}
\caption{Agreement (QWK, K=5, item means, bootstrap CIs) by model and reasoning mode, per dataset,
with guidance and one question per call. Reasoning-on bars use the reasoning samples (175 items per
public dataset); PT-CS has 379 validated answers.}
\label{fig:perdataset}
\end{figure}

These absolute levels are best read against the human reference. Mohler gives two teachers' grades for
every answer, and the two agree with each other at QWK 0.49. Every model agrees with their mean at 0.61
to 0.66; against each teacher separately, the models reach 0.73 to 0.80 with the first teacher and only
0.33 to 0.41 with the second. Agreement between teachers sets a modest ceiling, and one teacher sits
much closer to the models than the other.

Because SemEval's gold is a binary correct-or-incorrect label, the natural readings are accuracy and
AUROC (the chance a correct answer scores higher than an incorrect one), which suit it better than the
binned QWK of Fig.~\ref{fig:perdataset}. Across all SemEval items, with reasoning off, the models label
answers correctly 0.76 to 0.79 of the time, with AUROC 0.83 to 0.85, so the grader separates correct
from incorrect well above chance. The fixed 0.5 cutoff does not flatter these figures: for every model
it is within 0.024 accuracy of the best cutoff between 0.30 and 0.70. We do not break SemEval into its
seen and unseen subsets: those splits were defined for supervised systems relative to a training set,
and our prompted models have none, so the labels do not mark novelty to our grader.

Two readings turn this into guidance. First, how much the configuration matters depends on the task:
on short answers the eight configurations fall within 0.04 QWK of each other, but on code they span
0.26 (Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality}a and~b). On short answers almost any configuration grades about as
well, so the choice can be made on cost; on code the configuration is worth optimising, which is where
reasoning and model choice earn their keep.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq4_cost.pgf}
\caption{Agreement versus cost on the public datasets, one point per model and reasoning mode:
(a) short answers (mean QWK over Mohler and SemEval), (b) code (RIAYN). The horizontal axis is the
cost of 1000 grades in euros, on a log scale because costs span more than three orders of magnitude.
Points up and to the left are better. Cost is computed from the logged tokens at the providers'
billed per-token rates.}
\label{fig:costquality}
\end{figure}

Second, cost separates the configurations far more than agreement, and how that plays out depends on
the task (Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality}). On short answers cost spans more than two orders of magnitude
(\euro{}0.02 to \euro{}6.3 per thousand grades) for almost no change in agreement, so reasoning off is
the efficient pick: in Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality}a, the four models with reasoning off reach 0.60 to
0.62 at \euro{}0.02 to \euro{}0.34, while the best short-answer configuration, Qwen3.5 with reasoning on,
adds about 0.01 at about 200 times the cost of Qwen3.5 with reasoning off. Because the models with
reasoning off sit within 0.02 of each other, the choice of model matters little on short answers. On
code (Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality}b) the spread tracks effort, and reasoning is what buys it: on RIAYN it
lifted agreement for every family, significantly for two of the four (Section~\ref{sec:rq1}), and
GLM-5.1 leads at 0.726 with reasoning off (\euro{}0.95) and 0.803 with reasoning on (\euro{}6.4). For
Qwen3.5 the code gain (0.544 to 0.754) is mostly the repair of its zero-collapse, not a general
benefit. The closed frontier model is never the efficient choice: GPT-5.1 sits mid-pack on short
answers (0.609 with reasoning off, at about 20 times DeepSeek-V4-Flash's cost), and on code it reaches
0.791 only with reasoning, at \euro{}30 per thousand grades, the most expensive configuration in the
study and still below GLM-5.1 with reasoning.

GLM-5.1 is the efficient all-rounder: with reasoning off it is already the best code grader (0.726)
and near the top on short answers (0.619), both at under one euro per thousand grades. The dependable
rule is therefore reasoning off by default, on the cost argument that holds on every task. Reasoning
earns its keep only on code, and conditionally: it gives the study's best configuration (GLM 0.803) but
that gain is not significant, and across families the code benefit was significant only where it
repaired a collapsed baseline (Qwen) or on one dataset for GPT-5.1 (Section~\ref{sec:rq1}). So turn it
on for code when a model collapses or local validation shows it pays. The configuration guide
(Section~\ref{sec:framework}) builds this rule in and tests its default against the best configuration
on each dataset.

Cost also carries an operational lesson. All the experiments together (whole-exam cost counted once per
call) cost \euro{}101.1 at the providers' billed rates: \euro{}50.4 on OpenAI and \euro{}50.7 on
DeepInfra. Before running the core experiment matrix, the set of comparisons planned at the outset, we estimated its
cost by pricing every planned call at list price, using typical input and output lengths from pilot runs;
that estimate was \euro{}16.7, while the core matrix cost \euro{}59.8, 3.6 times more. On OpenAI, where the
budgeted price was right, the estimate was 1.9 times too low only because reasoning traces ran longer
than the pilots; the first reasoning runs even had to be repeated with the output ceiling raised eightfold
(4096 to 32\,768 tokens). On DeepInfra it was 4.4 times too low, because per-token prices below those the
provider billed compounded the same effect. Practitioners budgeting a reasoning-on grading arm should
price it at the provider's current billed rates and expect output several times longer than a pilot
suggests.

\subsection{RQ5: Conversation State}
\label{sec:rq5}

Grades can be shaped not only by how each answer is scored, but by how the whole grading session is
run. This sub-study varies whether each of a student's answers is graded in its own clean
conversation or inside one shared conversation that accumulates across that student's exam. Within
the shared conversation it also varies the order in which the answers are presented: the exam's own
question order, or the reverse. It needs complete multi-question exams, which only the deployment
provides: the public datasets are independent single items with no exam to share a conversation across
or to reorder. Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash graded 80 complete code exams five times each; GLM-5.1
graded the first 20 of the same exams three times. Everything else is held at the baseline
configuration. Because the sub-study compares the model's grades with one another across session
conditions, never with a teacher's grade, it does not need validated grades.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\input{figures/fig5_conversation.pgf}
\caption{Conversation sub-study, per model, with 95\% confidence intervals: (a) mean grade in one shared,
accumulating conversation minus the mean grade with a clean conversation per answer; (b) answer order
within the shared conversation, as the typical size of the change between the exam's own order and the
reverse (solid) and the average shift (hatched). Grades as a fraction of the scale. Qwen3.5 and
DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 80 code exams, $k=5$; GLM-5.1: the first 20 of those exams, $k=3$.}
\label{fig:conversation}
\end{figure}

Grading inside one shared, accumulating conversation lowered grades for every model
(Fig.~\ref{fig:conversation}a), but only slightly: by $0.012$ of the scale for Qwen3.5 (Wilcoxon
$p=.03$), $0.010$ for DeepSeek-V4-Flash ($p=.18$, not significant), and $0.027$ for GLM-5.1 ($p=.003$).
Answer order mattered more for individual grades (Fig.~\ref{fig:conversation}b): the same answer
scored differently depending on its position, by a typical $0.08$ of the scale for Qwen3.5 and
DeepSeek-V4-Flash and $0.10$ for GLM-5.1. On the 80 exams the order also shifted the average grade a
little, but in opposite directions for the two models: the exam's own order scored $0.013$ higher for
DeepSeek-V4-Flash ($p<.001$) and $0.015$ lower for Qwen3.5 ($p=.004$), while GLM-5.1 showed no shift on its
20 exams. Position therefore adds variation with no general direction. Because Qwen's zero-collapse can
hide order effects (an answer floored at zero cannot move), the other two models are the cleaner read.

Overall, how the session is run matters, more for individual grades than for averages. A shared
history pulled grades slightly down and answer order moved individual grades by about a tenth of the
scale, in a direction that depended on the model. Clean, question-by-question grading avoids both, which
recommends it on fairness grounds: a student's grade should not depend on where their answer fell in the
session.

\subsection{RQ6: Transfer to the Deployment Context}
\label{sec:rq6}

\begin{figure}[!b]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq6_transfer.pgf}
\caption{Transfer of the configuration ranking from the public datasets to the deployment context,
within each domain: (a) public short answers (mean over Mohler and SemEval) against PT-CS short
answers, (b) public code (RIAYN) against PT-CS code. Each line is one configuration (a model
with reasoning on or off); the vertical axis is agreement with the human grade (QWK, K=5). The public
ranking is computed from the public datasets only, with PT-CS held out of it. PT-CS items: short
answers 84 with reasoning off and 32 with reasoning on; code 295 and 67.}
\label{fig:transfer}
\end{figure}

The last comparison asks whether the configuration guidance found on the public datasets carries over
to a real deployment context. PT-CS, with its 379 teacher-validated answers from a live
AI-assisted grading platform, is that context. PT-CS has
already appeared in the earlier questions, but at the level of a single factor, asking whether reasoning,
guidance, or scope behaves on it as on the public data. The question here is asked once and at the level
of the whole configuration ranking: if you pick the configuration that ranks best on the public datasets,
is it the one that ranks best in deployment? Two choices keep the comparison clean. The public ranking is
computed from the public datasets alone, with PT-CS held out of it, so this is a genuine
out-of-public-sample check, not a re-reading of data that drove the ranking. And the comparison is made
within domain, public short answers against PT-CS short answers and public code against PT-CS code,
so short and code are never averaged together (Fig.~\ref{fig:transfer}).

The eight configurations, four models with reasoning off and on, can now be compared on both sides,
since GPT-5.1 graded the same items as the open models (Fig.~\ref{fig:transfer}). On code the order
carries over: the public and deployment orderings correlate at Spearman $\rho=0.81$, where 1 would be an
identical order and 0 an unrelated one, which is significant even with eight configurations ($p=.015$).
The public datasets spread the code graders over 0.26 QWK and so impose a real order: GLM-5.1 leads on
the public data and shares first place on PT-CS (its reasoning-off variant, 0.672, level with GPT-5.1
with reasoning), and Qwen3.5 with reasoning off, held down by its zero-collapse (Section~\ref{sec:rq1}),
is last on both. On short answers the order does not carry over beyond its ends ($\rho=0.36$,
$p=.39$). The public datasets separate the eight configurations by only 0.04 QWK, so most of the
public order is a set of near-ties, and the middle reshuffles on PT-CS; the extremes hold, with Qwen3.5
with reasoning on first and DeepSeek-V4-Flash with reasoning on last on both sides. Absolute levels shift
between contexts too, up on PT-CS short answers and down on PT-CS code, but transfer concerns the
ordering, not the level.

Overall, the configuration ranking transfers in the sense that matters most for a configuration guide:
the best public choice is also at the top in deployment, exactly on short answers (Qwen3.5 with
reasoning on) and at the model-family level on code (GLM-5.1). Below the top, the order transfers where
the public data separate the configurations clearly, on code, and not where they barely do, on short
answers. The practical reading follows directly (Section~\ref{sec:cost}): on code, a configuration chosen
on public data is a strong, transferable default; on short answers, where the configurations are close,
the choice matters less and is best confirmed locally.
